newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian cash promises said difficult for economy.
newsitem.headline: Serbian cash promises said difficult for economy.

text.p: The Serbian government has promised cash for students, workers and pensioners in an attempt to calm demonstrations after disputed elections and head off strikes over living standards.
But the economy can ill afford its generosity, analysts said on Thursday.
The socialist authorities said on Wednesday that electricity quotas which forced up bills would be scrapped in order to make energy cheaper.
The move will hit the government's income on top of promises to start issuing student grants this month and to pay pensions, due since October, with an added bonus.
Independent economists said the government would be forced to print money, despite the risk of inflation, to meet the payments.
"There are no dinars," said Jovan Rankovic, lecturer at the Belgrade University School of Economics. "There are no reserve funds. The only real source is the mint."
According to the government, tax revenues have increased and were more regular because of stricter financial discipline and measures taken to curb grey economy.
The analysts doubted the money collected this way would meet increased demands for cash but the government remained anxious to prevent the unrest spreading.
"Workers are demanding payment of overdue wages and the police, army and pensioners have received no payments yet," Stojan Stamenkovic, an economist at the Institute of Economic Sciences said.
"The government could reallocate some of the very small existing surpluses," he said. "But this would not resolve a permanent 30-40 percent shortage of cash."
Rankovic estimated about 900 million dinars ($175) a month was needed for pensions alone.
"Printing the money is the only solution for the problem to be quickly resolved," he said.

Zoran Popov of the Belgrade Institute of Economics said that if authorities resorted to printing money, "it means they think the situation is very critical for the stability of the entire country." -- Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
